Documents show lead azide concerns at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant date back decades

By Brian Tabick
Published: Nov. 24, 2026 at 12:02 AM EST|Updated: 5 hours ago
Add Us On GoogleAdd as a preferred source on Google
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 2:25
Instaread

MIDDLETOWN, Iowa (KCRG) - Court documents show concerns about deteriorating lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant date back decades, according to an i9 investigation by reporter Brian Tabick.

The documents do not answer what happened to the drums holding nearly 5 tons of lead azide.

What testing showed in March

Routine testing in March showed the ethanol and water bath had evaporated, which let the lead azide re-crystallize.

President Trump blames then-President Obama. The i9 investigation found documents that say the issue goes back further.

Expert wrote to the court

Dr. Ron Sahu, a combustion expert and environmental engineer, wrote to the court to supplement environmental groups’ lawsuit against the EPA. Sahu said he was concerned about what is happening at the plant.

“The decision making process has not been transparent,” Sahu said. “How were the risks assessed on the other pathways or other options and why was this the chosen option.”

Sahu said the Army knew it had problems dealing with lead azide. The explosive has been part of the plant since the 1980s.

An EPA report shows the Army had limited success neutralizing lead azide itself, chemically with an electric current.

Asked whether it was surprising that after 40 years of knowing about the issue the Army is still dealing with it the same way, Sahu said, “I won’t comment on their constraints and their priorities but obviously once it gets to place where you can’t kick the can down the road any more than you are forced to deal with it and your options have narrowed.”

2004 assessment cited deterioration

An environmental assessment from 2004 shows the Department of Defense was concerned about an old stockpile of lead azide that had been deteriorating for 40 years at the plant in Middletown.

Asked how long it takes lead azide to deteriorate, Sahu said, “Ordinarily, if you store it properly, it should not deteriorate. It should stay for a long long time. It’s only when the conditions of storage are not carefully monitored that it starts to form crystals and things of that sort.”

Cleanup contract ended

The Army hired a company in March to clean up the lead azide for about $120,000.

According to The New York Times, the contract was terminated two months later, before the job was completed. The Times reported the reason given was “safety concerns.”
